utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. I think I said yesterday that we'd sit in the same courtroom, but you all found your way to the right one. So even without the guidance of the Chamber, you get where you have to be. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to resume the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could I ask you to escort the witness and his counsel into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Counsel. Does counsel have earphones over there? Could we ask perhaps counsel to sit at the other side, because there's an extra set of earphones. I think if we would move Mr. Tomic to the other side. There's another set nearby, I think, Madam Usher. I see one on the table which gives a bit more room. Oh, that's just same distance. Mr. Tomic, you have no microphone, but you're so nearby that if there would be any need to intervene, then just draw my attention to that need. Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony last Tuesday. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before we adjourned yesterday, if I recall correctly, we were discussing that period of time during which you served as deputy minister for the Bosnian Serb MUP in 1992. I'd like to move ahead this morning to your work with the Ministry of Justice as minister of justice. And in that connection, I'd like you to take a look at Prosecution's next exhibit in order, which is 03025687.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P430, which is now before you, is a document dated the 1st of May, 1992, directed to the president of district assemblies for the Banja Luka, Sarajevo, Sokolac, Trebinje, Bijeljina, and Doboj regions. The subject is decisions in legislation and prosecution, and that document bears your name as minister of justice and apparently was signed for you. Let me give you a moment to look at that document, and then I'd like to ask you some questions about it. Do you need more time with that document, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. You may ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, was the distribution of this document essentially an attempt to begin the establishment of the organs of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it, therefore, addressed to the various organs under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in the paragraph marked -- or identified as number 1, you seek the commencement of establishing regular courts in various locales; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And number 2 addresses public prosecutors' offices and identifies the steps by which you seek the establishment of those offices and the beginning of their function.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And similarly, for the remaining portions of the document, in number 3, it focuses on the establishment of penal and correctional institutions on the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Number 4, the misdemeanour courts, and number 5, the channelling of fines for misdemeanours and implementing misdemeanour procedures during war and the imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And by this document, if I understand the first paragraph correctly, you were instructing the presidents of district assemblies that they were required to undertake the implementation of the steps necessary to establish those organs in conditions of war and imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me to explain. Before the war, in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were five district courts in five districts. Those were Bihac, Banja Luka, Doboj, Sarajevo, Zenica. Under the constitution of the Republic of Srpska, Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, five districts were established, at the head of which there should have been five district or higher courts which under the law on the courts should have detention units for these districts; that is, Banja Luka, Sarajevo, Trebinje, Banja Luka, and Doboj. That means that Banja Luka, Sarajevo, and Doboj were districts from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that had had their detention units attached to the district or high courts, as they were called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that identifies the areas in which those courts were intended to be established under the new Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and under the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that in the area of the Republic of Srpska, in addition to the old three districts and the old high or district courts, which dealt with certain serious crimes as first instance and then second instance in misdemeanours, Bijeljina and Trebinje were added to them. During the war, remand prisons were formed for those who were under the prosecution, or rather, correction -- under the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those also fell within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The establishment of the courts, my assistant, Slobodan Velasevic signed this document and he was my assistant for judiciary issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me ask you to next take a look at Prosecution's next in order. That's ET 0345-5967.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P431 is a document dated 20 May 1992, directed to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Justice, attention to the SJB under-secretary in the case of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and attention to the minister in the case of the Ministry of Justice. And it was sent by the chief of the SJB Novi Grad, Milenko Tepavcevic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tepavcevic was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. The subject of Mr. Tepavcevic's memo is information regarding accommodation, food, hygiene, and other problems of persons detained at KP Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Butmir, KP Dom Butmir, one of the facilities that was established during the course of beginning the Ministry of Justice in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The KP Dom Butmir had been existing for 50 years in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a semi-close type of prison for lighter sentences and for misdemeanours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So when the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established and the Ministry of Justice was established, it was one of those facilities that then came -- pre-established facilities that then fell under its jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This facility at the time was under the jurisdiction of the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, and there was also the SJB Ilidza there, and they addressed the under-secretary of the public service, security service. The man who was in charge of the public security in Republika Srpska, which could be described as third man from the top in this particular area in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know who that was in particular at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreter didn't quite understand your response.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I think his name was Cedo Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tepavcevic's memo is directed to the under-secretary for the Ministry of Internal Affairs. It's also directed to the minister of justice. For what reason was it directed to your attention?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry of justice in 1992 was supposed to take over this facility and turn it into a remand prison of the Sarajevo district court that was established in May 1992. Probably the reason that this was a facility under the jurisdiction of the judiciary, it should have remained after the takeover which took place in August 1992. And there's minutes of the hand-over between MUP and the judiciary, and probably this is why it was directed to the Ministry of Justice, describing the situation in the facility at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, under the jurisdiction of which department or ministry did KP Dom Butmir fall?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice and Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was the reason, at least according to you, that KP Dom Butmir was temporarily under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Internal Affairs because you were beginning the process of setting up the Ministry of Justice and it was intended that this facility would fall within the Ministry of Justice, just as it had done in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly what I said a while ago. We were in the process of establishing institutions of the Ministry of Justice. That means creating regular courts, high courts, lower courts, first-instance, and second-instance courts, and supreme courts. Under the law on judiciary, each district court was bound to have a remand prison and a detention unit for investigation purposes. It was agreed that this facility in 1992 should be taken over from the police and converted into an investigating unit of the district court of Sarajevo, one of the five district courts that existed in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was both under the constitution and according to the law on judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there a warden or equivalent at KP Dom Butmir at the time, on May 20th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that time there was no warden. I'm not quite sure. However, full jurisdiction of the administration of the premises and the guards around the prison was regulated by Milenko Tepavcevic, as the head, the chief of police -- the chief of the police force under whose control the premises was. And he was in charge of that particular facility on the 25th of May, 1992. And you can see that from this document and the date as it stands there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, item 3 of the memo of May 1st that you directed to the presidents of district assemblies requires the immediate submission of nominees for warden and deputy wardens of penal and correctional institutions. Were wardens appointed for KP Dom Butmir, or was a warden and a deputy warden appointed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I don't think so, and here's why. Because I was elected as minister of justice on the 19th of May, that is to say, one day prior to this document. And I cannot believe that wardens would have been appointed before my own appointment. That would be contrary to the law. And all these documents, just as the one you showed me a moment ago, were actually preparations for the creation of the Serb system of justice in Republika Srpska. They were all for the judiciary, et cetera. They were all preparatory to this, and I was the deputy minister of MUP, and it was my job to look at the cadres, materiel preparations, and so on, for a Serbian judiciary to be set up, a civilian Serbian judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was the first warden who you appointed for KP Dom Butmir?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Ratko Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you also appoint a deputy warden?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. But it was Soniboj Skiljevic, if there was one, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, on the document in front of you right now, Prosecution's 431, at the top of the memo we see the handwritten name "Ratko L." Do you know whether or not that refers to Ratko Lalovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Also, we can see at the top of the page, where the heading is, "SJB Ilidza SJB Novi Grad, SM" and then in parentheses, Kula. Was KP Dom Butmir also known as Kula?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, after you assumed the position of minister of justice, Mr. Mandic, where was your office located?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a time, my office was at Vrace, and when I was appointed minister of justice, the offices of the Ministry of Justice were at the Bistrica Hotel on Mount Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how long did the offices or headquarters of the Ministry of Justice remain at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until I was replaced and left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were there other offices of the Ministry of Justice, judicial centres, for example?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The higher court was located in the Kula facilities, where the police centre of Kula was located as well. The first-instance court was there and the second-instance court was there, throughout the time I was minister. I had an office, as minister, in one of the buildings in that general area, when I communicated with Sarajevo and when I had business to attend to in the city of Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just looking quickly at the content of Mr. Tepavcevic's memo regarding accommodation, food, hygiene, and other problems at Kula, in the first paragraph he identifies the number of persons who were detained between 12 May 1992 and 20 May 1992 on, as he puts it, various grounds. He then says that "preliminary operative interviews were conducted with these persons and lists containing all necessary personal data were delivered on time to the MUP." What was the nature of the preliminary operative interviews that were conducted of persons detained on various grounds at Kula?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say, because I wasn't informed about that. I didn't conduct those interviews. I didn't work in the MUP. I just prepared the road for the Serbian judiciary. This was conducted by the competent authorities, that is to say, the head of the public security service, down the line, down the chain of command, to Tepavcevic. So this was something that the public and State Security Services did, probably. And I say that on the basis of my experience. But as I say, I wasn't kept abreast of things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know the purpose of those preliminary operative interviews?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't informed about that, nor did I take part in any of those interviews or receive reports about the interviews. And it says here that all the facts were sent on time to the MUP headquarters and the public security services and the top man there. I think it was Cedo Kljajic at the time, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the last paragraph, Mr. Tepavcevic emphasises the inadequate conditions of accommodation, food, hygiene, and the state of health of the detainees, and emphasises the urgency in resolving their status.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Beyond this memo, did he communicate to you in any other way about the inadequate conditions at Kula?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The care and attention of these people was under the MUP. That was the police station, and providing exclusive security for these people, their exchange and everything else. That was all conducted by the MUP of Republika Srpska, led by this chief of police, Mr. Tepavcevic. I think the commander's name was Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, because -- well, let me ask you quickly: Did Mr. Tepavcevic have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Limun, or lemon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Mandic, let me ask you to turn next to Prosecution's next exhibit in order. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you're done with this document, I would have a few questions for the witness. Mr. Mandic, where this document says that these persons were taken into custody on various grounds, what did you understand what variety would be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't answer that and explain it, Your Honour, but I can just assume that it was from general crimes to prisoners of war or due to the effects of war where people were taken in for exchange later on. But that is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To take people in for exchange, what would be the legal basis for such custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't say, because I wasn't the responsible individual at that period of time for things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also said that they were taken -- perhaps taken into custody for crimes. Would crime investigations and prosecution fall within the area of responsibility of the minister of justice or any other ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it was from the area of general crime, yes, it would come under the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you say that this was not -- you said you were not the responsible individual. At the same time, you say that they might have been taken into custody for general crimes. Why, then, were you not responsible, at least for that part of the detentions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, we were creating the justice system, the judiciary, and I was appointed minister of justice the day before, which did not exist up until then, and it was my role to set up the courts and the judiciary institutions attendant to the courts of the first instance, second instance, and third instance. So nothing existed at all in the region, no courts, nothing like that. I was a minister without a ministry, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me draw your attention to another part of this document. It says 31 persons from Dobrinja I settlement were taken in during the cleansing by TO Kasindol forces on the 14th of May, 1992." What do you understand to be the cleansing by TO Kasindol forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it says quite clearly here that the TO, which is the Territorial Defence, were the Crisis Staff, local ones, of the local communes, who, in armed conflicts -- if you want me to explain this to Your Honours - they took into custody or disarmed the opposite side and put the people in the -- on the premises of the KP Dom Butmir, which means the army and the police, or rather, the Crisis Staff of the Territorial Defence, as it was called. The armed forces, in fact, of the Serbs from Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now a little bit higher up, it says: "38 persons were brought in by TO Ilidza Kasindol street. They were in possession of automatic weapons, were disarmed, and brought to KP Dom Butmir? That's different language that describes what happens, whereas a few lines further down, the word "cleansing" is used. Did that mean anything to you? Because the way you describe what cleansing is, is more or less what is described a few lines higher up, but then not by the word "cleansing."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe that it would perhaps, we suggest, be a good idea, with respect, to establish first of all whether this witness does in fact know anything at all about what the TO Kasindol forces did on the 14th of May. So that we are clear whether he is being invited to express some opinion on what the meaning of the word is or whether he's giving evidence about something that he actually knows about the events in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I asked the witness is how he understood this part of the letter that was addressed to him, and it's up to the witness to explain that, based on his personal knowledge of what happened. That's the explication of how he understood it. I'm asking you how you understood that and whether you have any -- whether it makes any difference to you, whether the word "cleansing" was used, on whatever basis you would have this interpretation. If you compare the word "cleansing" with the language used a couple of lines prior to that, the use of that word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know nothing about this event, neither did I take part in it. All I can say on the basis of my experience is to explain what I think this paper says, and I'm looking at this document for the first time now. I assume it was sent to the minister, to my assistant for the prisons, and his name was Slobodan Avlijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Stewart, you're invited not to intervene the way you did it a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I know why not, Your Honour? Because I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll tell you, not in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would Your Honour please tell me not in the presence of the witness, then, because I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask you: Could you please leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, what I wanted to elicit from this witness is how he interpreted this letter, either at that time, and my next question would have been on the basis of what he would have interpreted it this way, whether he had any personal knowledge or not. You intervened. You've drawn the attention of the witness to the possibilities that he might not have known or that he would have known. I wanted to elicit that from the witness even without your help. And that's the reason why I ask you not to intervene in a similar way next time. The witness may be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In future, then, I will undertake to be more careful that if I have such an intervention that might be unsatisfactory to present to the Court in the presence the witness I would make a request for the witness to leave court before I do it. I understand Your Honour's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, were civilians held and detained at Kula from the very beginning of its -- well, from the beginning of combat activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask the witness to look next at Prosecution's next in order, L0103023.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that Madam Registrar has a different document provided to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P432 is a document dated 28 October 1994. It's a memo to Mr. Ljubica Vladusevic and Mr. Dusan Kozic, sent by the Central Commission to the exchange of prisoners and civilians of Republika Srpska. And the subject is accommodation for Muslim civilians in KP Dom Butmir. The first line of the memo reads: "Since the beginning of combat activities in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, along with its basic purpose, Butmir KP Dom has also been used as location for accommodation of Muslim civilians passing through this facility in transit to the Muslim part of Sarajevo." The memo goes on to say that the facility was used for Muslim civilians in the process of "family reunification" or "freedom of movement" and it states that at the bottom of that page, according to rough estimates, about 10.000 Muslim civilians of all ages passed through this facility during the war, spending between several days and a few months in this facility. Mr. Mandic, do you have any reason to doubt either the accuracy of the estimate of the number of Muslim civilians of all ages who passed through the facility or the fact that that was taking place from the very beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this document dates back to 1994. At the time, I was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina, neither was I the minister of justice. On the 16th of November, I left Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was replaced as minister of justice, and I went to Belgrade. On the 8th of that -- in August of that same year, the Ministry of Justice took over this Kula facility as a remand prison and the hand-over and takeover was conducted. Ratko Lalovic and Slobodan Avlijas, that is to say, the warden of the prison and the assistant warden, were -- are the proper people to explain the way in which the prison functioned during the time I was minister and later on and the types of exchange that took place: how many people passed through the prison, whether they were civilians, whether they had been combatants or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was no suggestion, Mr. Mandic, that this document had been prepared at a time when you were minister or prepared at a time when Kula fell under your jurisdiction. I simply wanted to know if, based on your own experience, you had any reason to doubt the accuracy of the figures in here or the accuracy of the assertion that from the commencement of the war, civilians were detained in Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was signed by Dragan Bulajic, who was president of the Commission for Exchange, and I have no reason to doubt the contents of this document. And it was written towards the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can I ask you to turn next, then, to Prosecution's next in order, which is -- which will be the minutes of a meeting of the National Security Council on April 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P433, the document before you now, are the minutes of the meeting of the council for national security and the government held on 24 April 1992. Before I ask you about the contents of the document itself, let me ask you a couple of brief questions about the council for national security. First of all, did you yourself attend any meetings of the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who were the members of the National Security Council? Who comprised the council?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a body that was composed of ad hoc members, led by the president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Members of the council were probably the prime minister, the ministers of the interior and defence, and the president of the Assembly, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who presided over meetings of the council?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, if I could direct your attention to a portion of the meeting held on 24 April 1992. Under the heading "Decisions," about the ninth decision down, the minutes indicate that the council adopted the decision that the Ministry of Justice shall take over the exchange of prisoners once the organs of the interior have completed their work.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, were you present at the meeting at which that decision was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but probably I was, although I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what work was the Ministry of Interior to complete before the Ministry of Justice would take over the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Ministry of the Interior was supposed to conduct interviews and send the prisoners on elsewhere. Sorry, investigate the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Send them on elsewhere, investigate the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means to conduct the investigation and to collect as much information about the war and security and information that those prisoners could give them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Once the Ministry of Justice indicated it had completed its investigative efforts, what was the role of the -- sorry. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me begin that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Once the Ministry of Interior had completed its investigative efforts, what was the role of the Ministry of Justice then to be? What was the Ministry of Justice then to do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the government, a state Commission for Exchange was formed, involving one or two officials from the Ministry of Justice. They exchanged prisoners and held meetings with the other warring party for the purpose of exchange of POWs at various locations. I think that on behalf of the Ministry of Justice was present there assistant minister for prisoners and KP Dom. His name was Slobodan Avlijas. The government established this commission at the state level of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is that what was -- I understand that a state Commission for Exchange was formed, and we'll be directing our attention to that in a moment. But was the exchange of those persons who had been the subject of the Ministry of Interior's investigative efforts what was contemplated in the decision that was adopted on April 24th? In other words, on April 24th, 1992, when the National Security Council said that the Ministry of Justice would take over the exchange once the Ministry of Interior finished, what was contemplated at that time that the Ministry of Justice would do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the council decision and the government decision, a rather long period elapsed between this decision and the war, and it wasn't possible to communicate with certain areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a very laborious task of creating the ministry and a state. In certain areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, various groups were active, and there was a spillover of war from Croatia. Therefore, these conclusions were not easy to be implemented. It took a long time to establish power; to find out where the prisoners were, how they were held, and where; whether they were held by the army and the police; and only then could we establish the commission in order to take over the prisoners, inform the other party, most often that was Muslim party, and to effect the exchange of the people that were under their respective jurisdictions. You know, it was not possible to just adopt a conclusion and then implement it on the spot. We couldn't normally travel down the roads, because there was shooting, there was snipers shooting between Jahorina and Trebinje. It took us several hours to travel from Pale to Lukavica or from Pale to other parts of Sarajevo, which were criss-crossed and certain areas of Sarajevo were held by different warring parties. So we had a general problem of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I understand that in your response, you've directed your attention to the -- to alleged difficulties of implementation. What I had wanted to know was precisely what was contemplated by the decision of April 24th, rather than how difficult it may or may not have been to implement it. So let me ask you this, if I may. It may be quicker. Was the decision adopted on April 24th that the organs of the interior would investigate the captured or detained people, and then, once the Ministry of Interior was completed, the Ministry of Justice would conduct the exchange of those people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this meeting, the government passed a decision to establish a state commission. This commission was to be at the state level, not just under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice, but rather to be more efficient. In addition to people from the Ministry of Justice, other people were appointed, and I think the people were from MUP and from the Ministry of Defence, members of this commission. It was not solely the Ministry of Justice that was given the power to conduct exchanges, because we had tremendous problems on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn next to Prosecution's next in order. That's L0102734.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P434 is a report on the activities of the Ministry of Justice and administration in the May through October 1992 period. And it bears the date 16 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That is the time when I was the minister in the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I then direct your attention to certain parts of the document. First of all, can you turn to the third paragraph of the document. It appears on page 2 of the English translation, which states as follows: "Keeping in mind the demands for the successful establishment of the legal state and legal security of citizens, the ministry was forced to take a number of steps, primarily regarding the organisation of penal correctional organisation, mainly the Butmir KP Dom. Considering the increased influx of incarcerated persons and the need for this penal correctional organisation to be put to use, the ministry, therefore, urged the Presidency to establish a central commission for the exchange of prisoners of war, incarcerated and wounded persons, and dead bodies." First, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I take it that refers to the -- a Commission for Exchange that you mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the document mentions the increased influx of incarcerated persons and the need for the penal correctional organisation. Let me ask you a couple of questions about that. First of all, what was the extent of that increased influx of persons who were incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if it would be useful. It's not a particularly tendentious point, but just to establish first what involvement, if any, the witness had in relation to this report, whether it was to him, from him, et cetera, et cetera. He said he was the minister of justice. It's just on the face of it a Ministry of Justice report. It's -- I don't believe my point here goes in one party's direction rather than another. It just seems to be an appropriate practical step to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I do find it to be a tendentious point in precisely the way it was pointed out earlier in this day. I believe that in every jurisdiction it would be completely appropriate to ask the head of an organisation of this type about a document that reported on the activities of that organisation during a period of time --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting it's not, Your Honour. My point -- I'm completely puzzled. My submission is intended to be a totally harmless one. It's just a housekeeping kind of point. I don't disagree with what Mr. Tieger has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And some interventions should be reserved for cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How can I cross-examine on that? That's just ridiculous, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger [sic], the Chamber considers your intervention not as neutral as you suggested. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed in the way --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you mean Mr. Stewart there, Your Honour. I don't understand, Your Honour. That's my problem. I don't understand why it's not neutral. I assure Your Honour, it's entirely -- I don't understand how a similarity exists between that intervention and the previous one where Your Honour drew my attention to the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you have to live for a while without understanding this. At a later stage we can clarify that. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, returning to the question. That was simply if you could provide any information on the extent of the increased influx of incarcerated persons, and I think you were about to do so.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just explain to you. In August, when the Ministry of Justice took over the jurisdiction over the KP Dom, a large number of prisoners passed through and the guards and other employees of the Ministry of Justice just provided technical services, just, for instance, guarding and providing food for the detainees. However, the army had jurisdiction over these people, as well as the police did. They both came, conducted exchanges, and trials. As civilian ministries who had taken over the facility, just provided technical services, in absence of any possibility for us to effect in any way the exchanges. That is why we asked for this commission to become a state commission and that both members of the judiciary, the MUP, and the army be rendered responsible for the exchanges. In that way, we wanted to share the responsibility among everybody involved over these people detained there. I gave you precisely what the reasons were for establishing the Central Commission. We wanted to have some influence in creating the rule of law and legal security for those people who were mainly civilians from the war torn zones, and in a way they were provided shelter there. Mr. Prosecutor, if you allow me to explain further. The Ministry of Justice did not have military power. The guards there were unarmed, or rather, they did not go and visit the prisoners with weapons. We couldn't defend our principles of justice and fairness, either faced by the army or by the police. And in a way, we felt helpless in our attempt to put everything within a legal framework and legal norms. That is why we requested the Central Commission to be established and that everyone took their parts or their share of the responsibility for everything that was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next to Prosecution's next in order, ET 0124-6748.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, do you have the right document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit in order is a document dated 6 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's not the number you just mentioned, Mr. Tieger. Is that correct? And then it's a document dated the 6th of June. What I have in front of me at this moment are the minutes of a meeting held on the 9th of June. So I would be a bit surprised if that -- we'll then have now -- yes. Now I have a number in front of me -- a document in front of me which bears the number L0101953, dated the 6th of June. Please proceed. And that, then, would be P435.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a bit of confusion, I think. The Court has the right document, but it's an erroneous translation and we Have the correct translation is here. We'd like to substitute that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, in other words, the ERN number I recited earlier, the ET 0124, would be the correct exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although that's at the bottom of the page. So that's -- yes. The original bears that ERN number, and we now have a better translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So perhaps to avoid confusion we can return the erroneous translation and replace it with ET 0124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was presented to us as a draft translation now turns out to be a real draft and not ... So P435 now is the B/C/S original of an order dated the 6th of June, and P435 is the translation, not a draft translation. And that's P435.1. Mr. Tieger, I think we have sorted out the ... The witness now has in front of me P435? Yes. Then please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the logistics of the courtroom have certainly given you a full opportunity to look at this document. It is an order, as the Court noted, of 6 June 1992, and it's from the Central Commission of Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for exchange of prisoners of war, detainees, and bodies of the killed that are in the territory of the opposite side, and is signed by the president of the commission, Rajko Colovic. Did you know Mr. Colovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I knew him before the war and also during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Colovic's position before he became president of the Central Commission of Exchange?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, Mr. Colovic was assistant minister of the government for the prisons and KP, or rather, correctional and penal facilities of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the prime minister at the time was Jure Pelivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know the date on which he became -- the approximate date on which he became president of the Commission for Exchange?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. If I may, I would like to try and help you. After this meeting of the National Security Council of the government, where the decision was taken that the Ministry of Justice would establish the Exchange Commission, after that, at a government session, a state commission was formed involving various ministries, in order to fulfil the request posed by Mr. Colovic, referring both to the civilians and prisoners of war that were held by the armed forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say involving various ministries, does that mean that representatives of -- or employees of various ministries comprised the membership of the Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Colovic, for example, had been a member of or was a member of what ministry?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Either the Ministry of Justice or Defence. I know that he went from one to another, but I cannot say for sure at that particular time where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We can look at certain portions of the order that was issued by Mr. Colovic. The first paragraph of the order states that: "All the services of public security whose employees are engaged in safeguarding of facilities where prisoners of war or detainees are located shall keep evidence of all the persons who have been brought in. In addition to personal identifying information, this evidence must contain the information on the date and time when the person was detained, by whom the person was brought in, whether the person is wounded, and the time when the person was released or exchanged and upon whose order." So is it correct, Mr. Mandic, that that first part of Mr. Colovic's order is directed to members of the ministry of the interior who were involved in guarding or safeguarding facilities where detainees were held?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the third paragraph makes reference to municipal commissions for exchange and regional commissions for exchange, if any. So is it correct that the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- exchange system contemplated various bodies throughout Republika Srpska that would report to or provide information to the Central Commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the government took a decision to establish a state commission, headed by Mr. Colovic. The task of his and his closest associates was to establish at all levels, from the top to the lowest level, that would create a pyramid of commissions and to be accountable to the Central Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The fourth paragraph of the order states that "not any detainee or person deprived of liberty shall be either released or exchanged without prior order of the Commission for Exchange."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could ask you to turn to a paragraph about six paragraphs past the one we just focused upon. That states that "any case of injury or death of the detainees or persons deprived of liberty on the premises shall be registered and either official note or report shall be made thereof by a judge of the basic court in charge, in the presence of public prosecutor and a duly qualified staff member."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That, I take it, is another reflection of the involvement of -- we've already spoken about the involvement of the Ministry of the Interior. I take it that's a reflection of the involvement of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That involved investigation, where the Ministry of the Interior cannot conduct an investigation without the prosecutor, whether civilian or an army prosecutor or investigating judge. If it involves a member of the military personnel, then the investigation is done by the military judge and the military prosecutor. So these were two different jurisdictions, the civilian and the military, ones that were established at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, before we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I understand from Ms. Cmeric that the two references to investigation in that answer actually included the description on the spot, or that's what Ms. Cmeric suggests is the English translation, that -- there were two references where it was a compound phrase "on-the-spot investigations," the first and the second uses of the word "investigation."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Correct. The witness said on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, on-site. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Stewart, for your assistance. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Mandic, before we recess, let me ask you to turn your attention to a short paragraph about three paragraphs past the one we just looked at which states all complaints -- Your Honours, that's found on page 3 of the English translation. "All complaints relating to conduct and work of officials in charge towards detainees and persons deprived of liberty are subject to authority of an official of Ministry of Justice or the president of the higher or basic court.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the district court is in charge of that, whether it is a military court, a civilian court will depend on the person in question. The Ministry of Justice -- there is a civilian Ministry of Justice and a military ministry of justice. So depending on the person in question, whether it is a civilian or military person, then that will depend. So that's what I wanted to explain. And can you tell me what you mean? But in all areas, there were parallel courts, military and civilian. And their sphere of activity was separated, clearly differentiated. If an on-site investigation is conducted by a civilian court and then they find that it belongs to the realm of a military court, then an on-site investigation is conducted and a report sent in. If the military court goes out on an on-site investigation and establishes that it is -- involves a civilian, then it sends the report on to the competent authorities, the prosecuting offices or the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're past time for the break, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you dealt with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not -- I think not entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll wait. Mr. Mandic, we'll have a break until 11.00. I would like to see you back after the break. We adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Mandic. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as soon as I encouraged the Court to retain the document, in fact I realised that I was moving on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, then, I would have a few questions for you. In this document, there is a consistent use of language, making a distinction between detainees or persons deprived of liberty. Could you explain to us what the difference is, in your view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think there is any difference. Prisoners, or detainees, and persons deprived of liberty, I think it means the same. I can't explain the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it's consistently used, the language is different. Would you consider -- do you think that civilians who have not been suspected of any -- of committing any offence would be included in what you consider to be one category?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I can give a free interpretation, persons that have been detained, detainees, might have been people taken into custody as combatants and so on, whereas the others might be civilians or whatever. I don't know what Mr. Colovic thought of persons deprived of liberty, detainees or persons deprived of liberty. I think that the two are equated, that there's an equal sign there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "civilians," what civilians do you have in mind? Civilians under suspicion of having committed offences, or just civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both. As long as they weren't involved in any armed conflict, in armed combat, and so on, in the war; that they weren't apprehended with weapons, that they hadn't taken part in armed conflicts, in fighting, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they were deprived of their liberty on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't say, Your Honour, because this was done by the security services employees, and the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it was part of the exchange, I think, as far as I understood; representatives of your ministry were involved in the exchange of prisoners -- of the exchange of detained persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Detained civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So civilians were detained; they were deprived of their liberty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And again my question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's probably what they meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there was no suspicion of any offence committed by them, what would be the legal basis for deprivation of liberty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say for sure. All I can give you is my own explanation. Probably these people were on the territory where the war was going on. The civilians were taken into shelter so that the people shouldn't be killed, and then they were exchanged. But this was conducted by the members of MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But would you then say: We evacuated them? Or would you say: We deprived them of their liberty? Is that the same, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, who do you have in mind when you say "evacuate"? Which people? From which side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you say is that among the civilians that were deprived of their liberty, they might be persons that needed shelter because they were in the -- well, perhaps in the operational zones. That's at least how I understood your answer. You said the territory where the war was going on. I can imagine that you say it's dangerous here, so we should evacuate you, but the next step would then be to deprive them of their liberty. Is that the same in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, again the question: What was the basis for the detention or deprivation of liberty of ordinary civilians, not under suspicion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to make an observation in the absence of the witness in relation to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's only this: That at page 33, line 15, Your Honour put a hypothetical question to the witness, and my submission is only this, Your Honour: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just, since my system didn't function for a while, could you please read the part so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just disappeared off the screen of the I'll get it back. Ms. Cmeric will bring it back for me, Your Honour. Yes. Your Honour said, "If there was no suspicion of any offence committed by them, what would be the legal basis for deprivation of liberty." And Your Honour, my observation is a very short one. I submit it's very important that we bear in mind that in this line of questioning now of the witness stems from Your Honour's hypothetical question to the witness. He did not actually say that himself in evidence, so that the question Your Honour just asked at page 34, line 10, line -- so therefore again the question, "What was the basis for the detention or deprivation of liberty of ordinary civilians not under suspicion?" He didn't say that, Your Honour. That was the hypothesis in Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you what the basis for this assumption is. If you look at the whole of the document, you'll find "women whose detention or deprivation of liberty is not related to the war or war activities" on page 2. All the children and the minors up to 16 years of age." So I found it -- I found a sufficient basis for not only on the -- in the answer of the witness, but then -- perhaps I should not say again the question, but I'll come to that in a later case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In that case, if Your Honour was wishing it put it on the basis it wasn't a hypothetical question but on the basis of material which is considered to be sufficiently sound to put it to him as a fact, then we suggest that Your Honour should, with respect, move from hypothesis and put it very plainly to the witness so he understands the basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll do that, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought in again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, from this document, it appears that included in the category "detained persons or persons deprived of their liberty" that are included "women, where the deprivation of liberty is not related to the war or war activity, children, minors up to 16 years of age, old and helpless persons. Therefore -- because that's what the document says on page 3. I therefore again ask you the question: What was the legal basis for deprivation of liberty of those persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the territory of Republika Srpska, or rather, where the Serbs were in control, you had the crisis staffs of the army and the police. In certain municipalities or areas, what you had were the collection camps or prisoners. And among those collection centres, as we can see from this document, there were women and children there, and everybody who did not take part in the war. The purpose of setting up the commission was to differentiate between the prisoners of war who took part in the war and civilians who did not have anything to do with the war. So they were supposed to have -- the latter was supposed to have a different treatment and be returned to where they wished to go. So it was along these lines that Mr. Rajko Colovic, the president of the state commission issued this order and said that when the public security services -- that is to say within the MUP -- established who took part in the war and who did not took part in the war, that these two categories of persons should be differentiated and people should be deprived of their liberty on that basis. So that's how I understand this document, and it is a document that applies to the entire Serbian Republic or Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would all male persons between 16 and old age, in your view, be necessarily related to the war or war activities? I mean, could you imagine persons detained of 35, 40 years, 25 years, not related to war or war activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally think, Your Honour, that not all men took part in the war, not all males took part in the war. And it was up to the public security services to establish whether somebody did take part or did not take part. And of course, this order goes along those lines, to have people who did not take part in the war be released, or rather, sent to territories where they wished to take up residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then take -- ask your attention for, in the English version, page 3, but in the B/C/S version, I take it that it is -- let me just -- did you find the paragraph? It's approximately eight paragraphs from the bottom, where it says "all women whose detention, deprivation of liberty" -- you found that? It's approximately eight, linear, from the bottom. You found it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This paragraph seems to instruct to release women whose detention or deprivation of liberty is not related to the war or war activities, all children and minors up to 16 years, old and helpless persons, to be released. What about men being detained or deprived of their liberty, where this detention is not related to the war or war activities? Should they also be released or should they be kept or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, if you look further down the page where it says people who have been deprived of liberty, who are then prosecuted, this does not apply. So all males for whom it is established that they are not being prosecuted must have the treatment of free individuals and be placed at liberty. And it was precisely because of issues of this kind that a Central Commission was set up so that individual crisis staffs and para units or para-formations should not perform crimes against civilians and other people and that the rule of law and a legal state should be established on the Socialist Republic -- territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or Republika Srpska. And I think this illustrates the efforts made by the Serbian government by the state commission to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll put to you how I read this document at this moment and invite you to comment on that. The part you just referred to says that: "Detainees and persons deprived liberty against whom criminal proceedings have been started are not subject to this order, but to provisions of Criminal Code instead." I understand this to be that the mechanisms described in this document do not apply to them, which means that they are not under the competence of the Commission for Exchange and therefore, it shall be dealt with in a different way. I also read it that those against whom criminal proceedings have not been started are subject to this order; which means, and I'm drawing your attention to the fourth linear under the word "order," that they should not -- that they should be either released or exchanged, without prior order of the Commission for Exchange. Therefore, they should, up to that moment, remain detained or deprived of their liberty. I also read it in the contextual way, that the instruction to release women whose detention or deprivation of liberty is not related to the war or war activities, the instruction to release children and minors up to 16 years of age, and the instruction to release old and helpless persons, that this does not apply for males whose detention or deprivation of liberty is not related to the war or war activities and who are not minors or under 16 years of age and who are not old and helpless. That's how I read it in this context. But I'm inviting you to comment on that and to tell me what needs to be said about this way of reading the several parts of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're quite right, and your understanding of the document is correct. Now, how and in what way, I think that Rajko Colovic would be the person to explain that, because he was the person that issued, compiled this document on behalf of the state commission. It is my personal opinion that the possibility did exist on the Muslim side, that is to say, on the opposite warring side, that there were Serb males who had been arrested, captured, and that an exchange would take place between all parties on one side and all parties on the other side. And I think that's what it says in the penultimate paragraph of the document. And all-for-all exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me give confront you with the fact that this order was addressed or at least sent, as I take it from the bottom, to the minister of justice. Would you agree with that? Ministry of Justice, I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, Your Honour, it says "delivered to eight institutions." And I assume that the government discussed this issue; whether there were any comments or not, this was discussed by the government. So this is the first initial version of Rajko Colovic's order, who wanted to issue instructions about conduct with detained persons. On behalf of the Ministry of Justice, Slobodan Avlijas was in charge of that portion of the work. He probably received this document and he looked into it and collected all the proposals for any amendments that might be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, second part of your answer, you said the same happened on the other side. Would that, in your view as the minister of justice, justify the detention of civilians, even for purposes of exchange, who were not suspected of having --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- committed any offence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I don't think that would be justified, to detain civilians and hold them in custody. In the course of the war in 1992, I intervened on several occasions and prevailed upon the authorities to release some people, to have them go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you respond to the implications of this order when it was received at your ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that just now, but I'm sure that Slobodan Avlijas, my assistant for prisons, in charge of the prisons and prison institutions, did undertake to analyse the whole matter and that an answer was supplied at the government level, because this was a state commission, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no remembrance on the content of the answer given on behalf of your ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, because it was 12 or 13 years ago, and I really can't remember at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I do know that the conditions were improved from one day to the next and that the relationships was better between the Federation's commission and Republika Srpska's commission, that the way in which prisoners were exchanged was improved. So the standards were improved, and I think that the international community helped us, the CSE or whatever it was called, the ICRC or Red Cross, and we had very good cooperation with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'd like you to focus your recollection on the detention of males of - well, let's say anything between 16 and 60 - who were not suspected of any crime. Did you protest again, as it says here, detention or deprivation of liberty of that category of persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only myself, but the entire government, led by Mr. Djeric, asked that -- requested that people not be detained, that civilians not be detained or deprived of liberty who had been incorporated into the war. And this is evidenced by the minutes that the Prosecution has, and this was discussed at the Republika Srpska meetings, when it discussed the issue of conduct towards persons found on a territory who were not of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then draw your attention to another part of this order, where it reads: "Detainees and persons deprived of liberty may be used to work only in agriculture, industry, and mining industry; craftsmanship, except metalworks; mechanical and chemical industry; in transportation for loading and unloading, unless these have military loads or armament for trading." What was the basis for using detainees or persons deprived of liberty to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question, Your Honour. This is the first time I hear of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you interpret this line? How do you understand it, with your knowledge of the circumstances in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that this is a violation of human rights and the rights enjoyed by persons deprived of liberty, detainees. I do not consider that people who have been deprived of their liberty can be forced to do manual, physical labour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, I do understand that you interpret this paragraph as related to forced labour and not because they applied to work in mines or in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that people deprived of liberty cannot be forced, or even if legal proceedings have been undertaken against them, they cannot be forced to engage in manual, physical labour if they do not wish to do so themselves. That is against international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have been aware at that moment, since you say I hear it for the first time, although it's part of an order which is, among other addresses, also addressed to the Ministry of Justice and to the government. Would you have protested if you had been aware at that time as something that should not happen? I'm asking now for a judgement. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was informed that on several occasions, the army, or rather the crisis staffs, were looking for detainees and that was true on both sides, or rather, that they made them engage in manual labour, trench-digging and so on. And that is a problem faced by the government. And Mr. Djeric insisted upon the fact that prisoners of war of any kind should not be used for physical labour and should not be used for trench-digging, manual labour of this kind. And I think the Prosecution has a document to that effect. So I repeat: That was -- came up before parliament and was discussed by parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps we'll see that, but at this moment, we have a document in front of us signed by the president of the Commission for Exchange, which seems to accept the situation where detained persons or persons deprived of their liberty are involved in work, although only in limited sections of economic activity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we turn next to Prosecution's next in order, which I believe will be marked as P436. That's a document bearing the ERN Y001-0886 through 887, at least the English translation bears that. Mr. Mandic, I believe you referred earlier in your testimony to a decision by the government to form the Central Commission for Exchange. Looking at P436, I ask you whether that is the decision to which you referred.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that is a document dated 8 May 1992, signed by Professor Branko Djeric as prime minister, and entitled "Decision to form a Central Commission." And among other things, it announces that the commission will consist of a number of members, including the first named member of whom as the president - although there's a question mark by that in the English translation - is Rajko, last name illegible. Would that be Rajko Colovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you indicated earlier, the membership of the commission, as I specifically identified in the decision, includes representatives of the Ministry of Justice of the Ministry of Interior, and the representative of the National Defence Ministry?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm pausing, Your Honour, because I see the Court looking at the document. I don't want to rush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Tieger, my ears and my eyes are different organs. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I'd like to turn next to Prosecution's next in order. Those are the minutes from the government meeting on 9 June 1992, bearing the ERN ET 0124-5356.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would that be 5358, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P437, the document now before you, as I indicated earlier, is the minutes from the government session of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 9th of June, 1992. The heading indicates those -- indicates who chaired the meeting, some of those who were present, and also indicates those not present, including yourself. If I could direct your attention to a portion of the document found under what appears to be agenda item 1, or regarding 1, and that's 1B. That states: "The government acknowledged the letter of correspondence from the president of the central committee for the exchange of prisoners. It has been concluded that the minister of justice should talk to Rajko Colovic, the committee president, so as to determine what are the motives for requesting the change and to, if the reasons are justified, do the work of the committee president until a new president can be appointed." Now, Mr. Mandic, I understand from the minutes of the meeting that you were not present at that meeting, but were you made aware of the fact that Mr. Colovic had sent a letter to the government that apparently indicated his desire to leave the position of committee president, or commission president?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know - I talked with Mr. Colovic - he had personal reasons for that decision, to resign, because thereafter he was appointed the president of the court in Vlasenica. And after that, he became the judge of the supreme military court in Han Pijesak. I think that he cited personal reasons, marriage problems or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that you responded to the conclusion of the government that you should speak with Mr. Colovic about the letter he had sent and his desire to leave the commission.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did have this conversation with Mr. Colovic. And on that occasion, he explained to me that he was living in Han Pijesak, that he was to marry there, that he just had become a father, that he had become the president of the court in Vlasenica, and after that, the judge of the supreme military court in Han Pijesak. And I'm quite sure that his reasons were of personal nature, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And after making -- I take it, then, that you made a determination that his reasons were justified? Let me ask you: Did you make a determination that his reasons were justified and therefore undertake the work of the committee president until a new president was found, in keeping with the conclusion of the government on June 9th?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but surely this whole work was on the voluntary basis. No one could have been forced to do something that they didn't want to do. And I believe that his replacement would have been found very soon, whether it would be Slobodan Avlijas or anyone else. But I'm quite sure that his replacement, or rather, replacement for Mr. Colovic, was found very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And until that point, did you undertake the work of the commission president?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
