utterances.text: I never discharged the duty of the chairman of this Exchange Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you understand that it had been the conclusion of the government on June 9th that you should do so?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know who functioned as president of the commission between the time of Mr. Colovic's departure and the time that a replacement was found?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Prosecutor, but it says here that Colovic would discharge the duties of the commission president pending the replacement is found. In other words, it was concluded that the minister of justice should talk to Rajko Colovic, the commission president, so as to determine what his motives were for requesting a replacement, and if the reasons were justified, the above name - which means Rajko Colovic - would remain the president of the commission pending the appointment of a new president. So I was requested that he remains an outgoing president pending the appointment of his replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the portion of the document immediately above that, that is, 1A, it indicates that the government has supported the order of the Central Commission for the exchange of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just before we leave the previous point, it probably is just as well to clarify whether Mr. Tieger accepts what is in effect the witness saying that perhaps the English translation is potentially a tiny bit misleading, if one doesn't read it sufficiently carefully. Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if there's any translation problem, I'd like to invite Ms. Cmeric to read that specific part, have it translated by the interpreters, so that we can see whether there's any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. My point is, Your Honour, that we suggest that the question of Mr. Tieger put at page 47, line 10, which is just disappearing off the screen in a moment, "did you understand it had been the conclusion of the government on the June 9th that you should do so?" In other words, you should continue to act. We suggest it's now clear from the evidence that that is actually not a correct reading of that document. We just want it to be clear for the record. Certainly Ms. Cmeric can do exactly what Your Honour suggests and then we invite Mr. Tieger just to indicate whether he accepts that it -- well, I'll leave it neutrally, Your Honour, what he accepts as the meaning. Perhaps Ms. Cmeric could just read that bit of the B/C/S version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so, Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] "It has been concluded that the minister of justice should talk to Rajko Colovic, the president of the commission, in order to determine what the motives for requesting the replacement were, and if the reasons were justified -- the reasons for dismissal or -- were justified, the above named would discharge the duties of the president of the commission pending the appointment of a new president of the commission." [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I take it that there are no problems now any more with whatever translation. If you feel need to reformulate your question, do so. If not, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can we just be clear that Mr. Tieger is accepting "the above named" is in fact a reference to Mr. Colovic and not the minister? That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think it's incumbent on the Prosecution to announce its position on each and every point, particularly before the conclusion of an examination on -- related to that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, of course it is, Your Honour, because Mr. Tieger put a question on the other interpretation of this document, which, if that interpretation is correct, as we suggest it is, "the above named "means Mr. Colovic, then Mr. Tieger's question which he asked at that line reference I gave has to be withdrawn, because the question was based on a misunderstanding, a misreading. And of course it's incumbent on any counsel to withdraw a question if it's acknowledged and recognised that it's proceeding on the basis of a misunderstanding. That must be made clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A couple of points, Your Honour, first of all, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first read. One second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, as a minor matter, and I'm sure Mr. Stewart did not intend it, but this is not the first time that he's interrupted me in the course of a response. I just would like to ask that that not happen in future. I'd like to pursue this area. There are additional questions and additional documents related to that. I have no intention of pursuing a line of questioning based on a misunderstanding. Whether that misunderstanding can be clarified or not remains to be seen. Whether that area will remain somewhat ambiguous remains to be seen. I fully agree with the intention of anyone in this courtroom of clarifying the issues before the court insofar as possible, but taking a position with relation to this particular segment of the document at this time is premature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it can't be left in the air. We must have this resolved. It's a simple point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, what Mr. Stewart seeks is a correction, I take it, of the following part of your question: "Did you make a determination that his reasons were justified, and therefore, undertake the work of the committee president until a new president was found, in keeping with the conclusion of the government on June 9th?" Mr. Stewart, let me just ask you: Do you read that part as "therefore undertake," you understood that to be that you make a determination that his reasons were justified and that therefore you undertook the work? Is that how we have to read that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I need to go back to the original question. The point is this: Mr. Tieger put a question to the witness on the clear basis that that document was saying that it was the witness who was to undertake the functions of president of commission in the interim period. It now appears, Your Honour - it's not an unrealistic interpretation of what's happened -- it now appears that's completely false. We can't leave it in the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how you understood the question. I'm just trying to seek clarification Mr. Tieger in your question I think you suggest, the wording of your question, especially the words "and therefore undertake the work of the committee president" and you added to that "in keeping with the conclusion of the government on June 9th," which seems to indicate that you have interpreted the last couple of lines on the first page to charge the minister of justice with taking over temporarily the duties of the committee president. Is that how you read that, or -- I mean otherwise the reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That interpretation -- right. That is a correct reading of the interpretation, and I'm not withdrawing that interpretation. And now I'd like to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes: You may move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I say just one sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here that the minister of justice should talk to Rajko Colovic and that Colovic was supposed to explain his reasons. And if you use the term "the above named," and the only above named person in his paragraph was Rajko Colovic, should be nominated pending the appointment of a new president, provided his reasons were justified; if they were not justified, he must remain in this position. In no way whatsoever does this phrase refer to me, because Rajko Colovic was the only above named person in this paragraph that deals with his resignation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The matter has been sufficiently clarified at this moment. You may proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I be clear. May I remind, with respect, remind the Trial Chamber and Mr. Tieger, this is Mr. Tieger's witness. Does Mr. Tieger now accept that last answer and interpretation of the witness? Because if he doesn't, then he's rejecting the answer of his own witness, and I really am entitled to know right now whether he's rejecting the answer of his own witness rather than leave it up in the air for me to come back to at some future point in cross-examination. It's a simple point. What is Mr. Tieger -- what is the Prosecution's position, having had that clear answer from their own witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the question is whether you accept the answer of the witness or that you take it that it's inconsistent with the text of the document in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me answer that with three points, Your Honour. First of all, I think I've made it clear there's additional evidence that I intend to adduce that may shed light on this very issue for the Court, for counsel, and for the witness himself, number one. Number two, Mr. Stewart may come from a jurisdiction where, when a witness is called - and I don't know that to be the case - the Prosecution becomes -- that witness becomes, in effect, the Prosecution's witness. But as the Court is aware, the Prosecution will call before this court individuals from various -- from both sides of the conflict, from various parts of the government involved in the conflict, in an effort to bring to the Court as much information that may assist the Court as possible. And it's not a matter of putting the Prosecution's assertions to the Court through individual witnesses; it's a matter of bringing those witnesses in and adducing as much truthful information as possible through those witnesses. And finally, I thought I had made clear my current interpretation of that portion of the document. If it will assist counsel's cross-examination before he begins it, with respect to that particular document, after all the evidence has been adduced in direct examination, that's another story. But to spend more time on this at this point seems to me unproductive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's a general point of importance here. I don't come from a jurisdiction where anybody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Stewart. I am going to stop not you, but the parties, this debate at this moment doesn't assist the Chamber. Where there's any issue that would need clarification as to the position of the Prosecution in relation to answers given by a witness and the consistency with documents, which I fully acknowledge could be of importance for you to cross-examine the witness, unless there's any need to have them immediately resolved, where I do not see that need at this very moment, they could be dealt with at the end of a hearing. So I do agree with you that it's useful to have these matters clarified. At the same time, it should disrupt at a minimal level the flow of evidence. And therefore, the question stands. Let's wait whether it still stands. Because Mr. Tieger has indicated that we'll hear additional evidence which may cast a different light on that, and then at the end we'll see whether you need an exact clarification of the position of the Prosecution in order to prepare for cross-examination. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two questions before we leave this document, Mr. Mandic. First of all, with respect to 1A, that is, the portion of the document that reads: "The government has supported order of the central committee for the exchange of the prisoners," does that refer to the order of June 6th that we looked at previously that was Prosecution's Exhibit P435, the order of June 6th?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Second question, Mr. Mandic: Can you recall if at some point between Mr. -- between the time Mr. Colovic indicated he wished to resign and the time that a replacement was found, that you effectively undertook responsibility to be the -- to head the Exchange Commission or be the point position for the Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Might it help if you were able to listen to an intercepted telephone conversation that occurred during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like then, Your Honour, to turn to Prosecution's exhibit next in order. That's a telephone conversation between Nenad Vanovac and Mr. Mandic, held on the 23rd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P438, for the audio, and P438A for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, although the text is scrolling, I do not hear neither the original language nor any translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We may need some assistance from the booth. Would it be -- and I'm directing this to the booth, I guess. Is it of assistance if we begin the intercept once again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's restart it and see whether we get sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Unidentified Woman: Good afternoon. Is that Kula? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Unidentified Woman: This is Ilidza. Just a moment. Nenad Vanovac would like to speak to you. Nenad VANOVAC: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Nenad VANOVAC: Good afternoon. Momcilo MANDIC: Good afternoon. This is Vanovac. Nenad VANOVAC: Well, who I'm going to talk to in the future? I can't find this Elez anywhere. Momcilo MANDIC: Forget Elez. Everything is here with me directly until I find and the right men. He's a fool. Don't talk to him any more. Nenad VANOVAC: Well I did tell Rajko Colovic something along the same lines. Momcilo MANDIC: But Rajko's betrayed us, fuck him, everything is ruined there and ... the idiot. And today -- I will ... no, I can't today, tomorrow I'll find the right man, the day after tomorrow. I won't run [as interpreted] until a suitable one is found and that will directly ... I'll be the point of contact, of assistance. Nenad VANOVAC: Well, you know what, that man should be based either at Kula or here. Momcilo MANDIC: He'll be here at Kula with us or in Ilidza, it doesn't matter. We'll figure it out. Nenad VANOVAC: Okay, This is the problem. They called me about the eight you approved for the exchange with Hrasnica and Kolonija. Momcilo MANDIC: All right. Nenad VANOVAC: Nijaz Sukric... of the eight, there are, they told me that only two remain, Nijaz Sukric and Ibrahim Dzenanovic. Momcilo MANDIC: All right. Nenad VANOVAC: And now they want them. And they would free Vaso Rajak's brother, our priest here from Bijelo Polje and his brother-in-law, what's his name, I have them written down here. They would also free Pero Rajac from the Zenica KPD. Momcilo MANDIC: And where are those two men now? Nenad VANOVAC: At the Zenica KPD. Momcilo MANDIC: Right. Right. And where are the ones on the other side? Nenad VANOVAC: The ones on their side? Well, I wanted to ask if they're at Kula or ... Momcilo MANDIC: Can you please call our police station down here. They have the list, so they'll tell if you they're in Kula or in Lukavica. Nenad VANOVAC: I'll do that. Momcilo MANDIC: Please do. Nenad VANOVAC: I will. I'll talk to you later. Momcilo MANDIC: Yeah. Tepo has the list. Have him check it. Nenad VANOVAC: OK. Momcilo MANDIC: Talk to you later. Nenad VANOVAC: Bye. Momcilo MANDIC: Bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: According to our unusual procedure, I have to inquire whether there are any inconsistencies in the words spoken. If not, please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I asked you before the intercept was played whether it might be of assistance in recalling whether or not at some point you assumed a position as point of contact for exchanges to listen to a conversation that occurred at that time. Was it of assistance to hear this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for me to listen to the conversation again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand your conversation with Vanovac, you indicated to him that Rajko had betrayed, you say "betrayed us" there, that you will find the right person and that until a suitable one is found, then -- you said I'll be the point of contact of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Rajko went to Vlasenica and that he left an empty space. Now, as I happened to be down there when Mr. Vanovac called and there was the exchange of these people couldn't be put off, I stepped in and talked to Vanovac and it was urgent. The exchange had been urgently agreed upon. And I did my best and said that I could assist in these exchanges, that is to say, to have people go to one side and the other for the problem to be solved. As minister of justice, it was my goodwill. I wanted to speed up the whole business and complete the operation. So I did that of my own free will, not to have to wait until the new president of the state commission to be elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you refer, or in the conversation, you and Mr. Vanovac speak about Mr. Sukric and Mr. Dzenanovic, two of the eight who remained. Who were Mr. Sukric and Dzenanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know where those people were, because in Lukavica you had the military prison in Lukavica and at Kula was the other prison that came under the jurisdiction of the MUP, the security service. And at a certain point, I said: Well, Tepo has the list. And Tepo is Tepavcevic who we discussed a moment ago. He was the chief at Ilidza who had control of Kula. So I didn't know who was where, who had civilians, who had military personnel and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the question was whether you knew who they were, not where they were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vanovac indicated that you had previously approved their exchange as part of an exchange with, as you said it, "this is the problem. They called me about the eight you approved for the exchange with Hrasnica and Kolonija." So is it correct that before Mr. Vanovac's call on June 23, you had already approved an exchange with Hrasnica and Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think he meant me personally, but the state commission. Because I was not in charge or I did not conduct the exchanges. People from the state commission did, the commission set up at government level, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why would Mr. Vanovac have specifically identified those individuals by name to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember how this actually evolved, but as for the municipal commissions, they thought the state commission was the same as the government, the Ministry of Justice, and they interpreted it this way: You gave your agreement at commission level and they conducted the exchange. I think they meant the Central Commission that decided, based on Mr. Colovic, et cetera, and the decisions decided upon by the previous government. So it wasn't personal. It wasn't me personally. It was the state commission and government, and they personified me as embodying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we move to Prosecution's next in order. That is the document that bears the ERN ET 2097-7173.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P439 is a document which bears the heading "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence, Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners and Detainees," and is signed by the state commission chairman, Filip Vukovic, and is directed to the Central Commission for the Exchange of Persons. Is that a document regarding the exchange which was sent by the commission for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to its equivalent commission on the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And are you able to date that document through the fax on the -- the fax title on the first or second page -- or third page, for that matter? It appears to be a document that was faxed on the 26th of June. I think you can find those fax designations at the top of each page.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we see on the first page of the original document, that is, the B/C/S, the handwritten name Ratko. Do you know who that refers to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be Ratko Lalovic, who was the first head of the KP Dom. Actually, I'm not quite certain who that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the document bears a list of names. The first list is 35, the second list is 10, the third list is 15, the fourth list is 14, and then we see some names listed in the paragraph after that. That's at the bottom of the second -- the bottom of the second page of the document in B/C/S. Do you see the names Nijaz Sukric and Ibrahim Dzenanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And are those the same gentlemen referred to in the June 23rd, 1992 conversation between you and Mr. Vanovac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we next move to Prosecution's next in order. That bears the ERN 03091644.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P440, now before you, is a document from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of Justice, dated 4 July 1992, bearing your name and the indication that -- and a signature, but signed for you, it appears. Was this the appointment of Mr. Vanovac as president of the Central Commission to replace Mr. Colovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next exhibit is marked ETR 002-9604.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P441 is a document entitled "Agreement on Mutual Release of the Prisoners along the Line 'All-for-all'," and indicates it is based on agreement concluded on the 5th of July, 1992, signed -- and it's signed by Nenad Vanovac, B. Kelly, and Mr. Vukovic. And it consists of the agreement which is indicated generally on the first page of the English translation and then more details that follow and that are enumerated and that bear the names Radovan Karadzic and Alija Izetbegovic. On that document we see a signature -- signature lines for Mr. Karadzic and -- we see signature lines for Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Vanovac, and Mr. Vukovic, and we see signatures for Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Vanovac. Are you familiar with this document, sir, or at least the agreement that it reflects?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that an agreement was concluded on July 5th of this general nature and whether or not any exchange of prisoners resulted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of this document or the agreement, and I've never seen it before. This is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to look at this -- have you had a sufficient opportunity to look at this document since it's been placed in front of you? I'd like to at least give you an opportunity to look it over.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document states in part, in number 2, that: "In the presence of UNPROFOR representatives on 11 July 1992, at 12.00, both commissions will exchange the lists of prisoners requested by each side."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask you if generally you're aware of the participation of UNPROFOR representatives in efforts to facilitate or assist in agreements to release prisoners or detainees.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the work was done by Slobodan Avlijas on behalf of the Ministry of Justice. He was my assistant and he kept the records and was in charge of everything with respect to prisoners and prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier, I think, that in reviewing some of the documents related to the Exchange Commission, that lists were prepared and you referred to lists in your conversation with Mr. Vanovac. Are those generally the lists that appear to be referred to in item 2 of this document? That is, lists prepared to be exchanged so that detainees and prisoners would be released and exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify something here. I talked to Mr. Vanovac when he asked that the people -- that the exchange of these people be continued, people at Kula or Lukavica. I did not know about the subject matter, what it was about. I asked where the people were and how the exchange was being conducted. So I didn't compile any lists, nor was I aware of any lists. All the lists were kept by the people that were in charge of the Kula and Lukavica facilities. Lukavica was held by the army, Kula was held by the police. And in talking to Vanovac, I told him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were aware of the -- or were you aware of the existence of an Exchange Commission or some kind of commission that had -- that was engaged in the process of exchange on the part of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? That is, did you know there were equivalent commissions on both sides?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about that during the war and I was even a member of a commission myself in 1994, for example. It was commission for cooperation with UNPROFOR, and that's when I got to know those people at Butmir airport, the people who were members of the state commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you aware of how the exchanges were generally to take place and generally to be arranged? Did that involve the exchange of lists by both sides, the submission of a list by the commission for -- on behalf of Republika Srpska, and the submission of a list by the representatives from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I never took an active part in the work of the Commission for Exchange, on either side, which means that everybody else from the regional and municipal commissions sent lists to the Central Commission, which already numbered several members. So this conversation with Vanovac is something that happened to me at Kula. I happened to be there and I gave my agreement not to have to wait for anybody else and to slow up the process of the exchange. So I don't remember that I myself compiled lists in any way. I was the minister of justice. I had other affairs to see to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's 12.30. I can pursue this, but we may be discussing it for at least a few minutes, so it might be an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first have a break. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom. May I take the opportunity to draw the attention of the parties to the fact that the Chamber is still waiting on whether the parties would agree on how to -- what witness to hear on the 6th of December. I was informed that the question on whether Mr. Bjelobrk would have to reappear for further cross-examination, that that was a -- that that question was in view of the parties waiting for an answer by the Chamber. But I think the Chamber invited the parties to see to what extent they could agree on any of the paragraphs that were mentioned by the Defence as relevant for further cross-examination. So the Chamber would like to receive that information as soon as possible, and, of course, finally we'll decide whether or not it's necessary to have Mr. Bjelobrk recalled for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I say, Your Honour, I'm quite sure - I would probably just need to check outside court, I'm sure we can give Your Honour a very quick answer on the first point, which is what witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to invite you -- the witness is now in. I used the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Very quickly, Your Honour, I'm sure we can give Your Honour an answer on the first point. The second is likely to take longer. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. I'd rather now first give an opportunity to Mr. Tieger to resume his examination-in-chief. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can Exhibit P39 [sic] be presented to the witness again. Leave P41 with the witness for the time being as well. Sorry. P439. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, unless my numbering is incorrect, P439 is the document sent by Mr. Vukovic, as state commission chairman for the Exchange Commission for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's the -- he's on the -- that's the document bearing the heading "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence, Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners and Detainees"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, on the bottom of the second page, as we discussed before, we see that Mr. Vukovic provided the names of, among others, Nijaz Sukric and Ibrahim Dzenanovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as we discussed before, those were two persons in detention in Republika Srpska who the commission, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina commission, wanted to have exchanged; correct? In other words, Vukovic was seeking the release of, among others, Sukric and Dzenanovic and that's why their names were provided.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition, Mr. Vukovic provided lists of names of other persons believed to be held in detention in Republika Srpska and whose release he sought.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could have marked next in order, Your Honour, a document entitled "List of people who were captured," and bearing the ERN ET 0031-7099.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, if the witness could keep the other exhibits with him, meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, if I could ask you to look quickly -- first of all, yeah, let me ask you to look quickly at Prosecution's 441. That's the agreement that was based on an agreement concluded on July 5th, 1992. That's the document you were looking at just before the recess. Do you have that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please take care that the witness has P441 in front of him. The request has been by Mr. Tieger to leave these exhibits with the witness for a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we had looked previously at item 2 on that agreement, Mr. Mandic, that stated: "In the presence of the UNPROFOR representatives on 11 July 1992, both commissions will exchange a list of prisoners requested by each side." So that would be, I take it, lists similar to those presented by Mr. Vukovic in the document you just looked at, that is, lists of persons believed to be held in detention by the other side and whose release was sought.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking at P442, which is entitled "List of people who were captured," and bearing on the last page the signature of the president of the commission, Mr. Brkic, and what appears to be the seal of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would that be the kind of list submitted by the Muslim side indicating the names of the people whose release they sought, pursuant to these agreements and exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could turn your attention back to P439. That's the document sent by Mr. Vukovic. In addition to the individuals whose names appear in the body of the document, the lists that we discussed earlier, after Mr. Vukovic's signature there appears the indication "attachment, list of prisoners from 1 through 3.441." And earlier in the document, Mr. Vukovic indicates that the attachment contains the list of imprisoned persons and detainees according to our records. And again, Mr. Mandic, is that a reference to and the same kind of list we've been referring to, that is, the lists of persons believed to be held in detention by, in this case, the Muslim side and whose release was sought? Essentially the same kind of --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. I don't mean to make this a difficult question. I'm looking at this -- at the indication of a list of -- attachment, list of prisoners from 1 through 3.441. We've looked at earlier lists. Is this essentially the same kind of list?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a list here which says 1.931, and not 3.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I understand that, and that's -- I'm not suggesting that that was the precise list. I'm simply asking whether Mr. Vukovic's reference here to the attachment is a reference to essentially the same kind of list that is Prosecution's 441 and that is submitted for the purpose seeking the release of those people who were believed to be in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just say, we believe the Prosecution is a bit mixed up, but in the light of earlier observations, I say no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. Well, certainly that appears to be an improper reference to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So again, I'll repeat that question. We discussed the names that appeared in the body of Mr. Vukovic's list. We discussed the list of names that appear in P442. I'm simply asking you if the attachment in Mr. Vukovic's document is essentially the same thing. Not identifying the identical people, not the identical list, but a list submitted for the same purpose and pursuant to the same understandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could a bit helpful. Page 68, lines 5 to 9 we believe contains a complete misapprehension about the documents in question. Your Honour, it's the reference to the Muslim side in line 8. We believe that this list is people held by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. And I think the line -- I think what I asked the witness is, and maybe that is the source of the confusion, Mr. Mandic, and I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me just ask you: You see that in the bottom of P439 there is a reference to an attachment, "List of prisoners from 1 through 3.441." In P442, we have a list of prisoners, lists, as far as I understand, the Prosecution puts it to you that they are instrumental for exchange of prisoners. Would you consider the attachment list of prisoners from 1 through 3441 to be a similar list as the one in front of you under number P442?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't got that list, I think, 1 through 3441, have we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Therefore, I'm a bit surprised. I mean, if the witness doesn't know about that list -- but of course, Mr. Tieger, if we have a list of prisoners 1.900 and another one says list of prisoners 3.400, is there -- would the parties disagree that that would be also a list with names of prisoners which are presented in the framework and the context of prisoner exchange or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't seen the list, but the point is that when Mr. Tieger, at lines 5 to 9, I think it was line 8 specifically, when he said "by in this case the Muslim side, "which was an assertion included in the question -- we understand this list to be a list of people asserted to have been held by the Serb side. So it's potentially extremely confusing for the witness, and I've got to say, everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand counsel's point. There's no disagreement. It's only a matter of the way in which the question was phrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Try to phrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the Muslim side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In such a way -- Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from -- of course, I leave it to you how relevant this specific question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll try it once more and then we'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify any ambiguities, let me recap it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, Mr. Vukovic, as you indicated to us earlier, asked for the release of numbers of people who were held on the Serb side, including, as you indicated, Mr. Sukric and Mr. Dzenanovic, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must try and clarify my position, or rather, the fact that this is the first time that I'm seeing these documents. And the fact that I never engaged in exchange of POWs in 1992. This telephone conversation was my ad hoc assistance to this man to exchange two individuals, each from the Muslim and the Serbian side. And I charged Tepavcevic with this, who was the chief of the police station in Kula, to see to that matter. I never had any insight in those problems, nor was I in any way actively involved in compiling these lists in exchanges and things like that. So I don't believe I can be very helpful, I'm afraid. But I am at your disposal to tell you whatever I know. So I am a little bit perplexed. I don't know who this person Vukovic is, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't believe I'll be asking you at this point for any details about those lists that will take us beyond the answers you've already been able to provide. So if I ask you this question, it's only to provide the backdrop to my last question about -- to clarify the document. And as I say, you've already indicated to us that Mr. Vukovic submitted names of people held by the Bosnian Serbs and whose release he was requesting. That we agree to; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, as this document reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then you also indicated to us that this document with the list of many names, signed by Mr. Brkic, and that's Prosecution's 442, is a similar list; correct? That is, it's a list of persons held on the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so to avoid any further confusion, all I was asking was whether Mr. Vukovic's reference to an attachment with list of prisoners that appears after his signature is essentially the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. Do you think that this is part of this list of 3.000-plus people?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. It's essentially the same type of document, that is, requesting -- compiled by the Muslim side, of persons who are held in detention on the Bosnian Serb side and whose release they are requesting.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should indicate for the booth that the Prosecution's next exhibit in order is an intercept. It appears in Sanction. I think they need to know that in order to avoid any technical difficulties of the type we encountered before. And that would be ET 0322-0954 through 0959, at least the English transcript of that. And it's a conversation between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Krajisnik, on the 6th -- on the 25th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The audio will be Prosecution Exhibit P443, and the transcript, P443A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I should have alerted the registry to this earlier. This is an intercept that already has an exhibit number; that's P292, KID 3146G [sic]. I'm sorry. My apologies. Let's try it again. P292, KID 31469.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The audio can be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Milijana: Hello. Unidentified female: Yes. Milijana: Hi. Unidentified female: Hi. Hi. We've been waiting. Milijana: Has he arrived? Unidentified female: Yes. Just a minute. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes? Milijana: Hello. Good morning, Momo. Milijana speaking. Momcilo MANDIC: Hello, Milijana. Milijana: How are you. Momcilo MANDIC: Well ... Milijana: President Krajisnik wants to talk to you. Just a moment. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: What's new, Mandic? Momcilo MANDIC: Mr. President, how are things? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I must tell you, did you have the hiccups just now? Momcilo MANDIC: [Laughing] Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I just said that you are a real hero. All the others are just useless. Momcilo MANDIC: You are right in that one and for the rest we will see. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Useless, I must tell you. There are just few Serbs with such name and that reminds me of Vojvoda Momcilo. Momcilo MANDIC: [Laughing] Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Listen Momo... Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, tell me. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Milos Savic's brother has been arrested. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And now, listen to this. Momcilo MANDIC: Mr. President. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: The first part has been mopped up. It was done today. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Did they leave? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. It's been mopped up. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Huh? Momcilo MANDIC: The first part has been mopped up. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Which part. Momcilo MANDIC: That one, the one that was uncertain. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I don't know which one. Oh, the one up there? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: On the top, is it? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No kidding? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, and the men, they've already been transferred there. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Is that right? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, they're working. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Oh, good, excellent. I have to tell you, this is for your ears only. This, that I am giving you compliments, just to know that the bill for the commercials is on its way to you. Momcilo MANDIC: [Laughing] Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Listen, please. Milos Savic has been arrested. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Since are in that commission, Savic Dusan ... Momcilo MANDIC: Okay. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And now ... Momcilo MANDIC: Savic Dusan; is that right? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He is up there in that Knezevica potok, but his wife, sister-in-law, and his sister are there with him too. Momcilo MANDIC: In which "potok"? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You know, that is the Knezevica potok. Momcilo MANDIC: Where is that settlement? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: It is up there higher than Boljakov potok. Momcilo MANDIC: And Boljakov potok? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Between Buca potok and Boljakova potok. Momcilo MANDIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: But let me tell you, Savic Dusan has been arrested. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: But please if you can, when you have time to contact them, you are in that commission, you know... Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Make a contact because his wife and all the other here are going insane. Momcilo MANDIC: Okay okay we will put him on a list for tomorrow. Done. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And what, tell me is it in a that part? Yesterday when we were looking at that portion that was not clear, is that it? Momcilo MANDIC: Oh yes, that past closest to me. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Okay, good. Momcilo MANDIC: That has been done. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And tell me that, that stronghold, has it been put together? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I must tell you that you will be decorated, when the circumstances are right, you'll get a medal... Momcilo MANDIC: It's the people that did it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Oh, yes. Momcilo MANDIC: These, these specialists of mine. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: They are not many like that. Momcilo MANDIC: And if they are ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Just go ahead. Momcilo MANDIC: Agreed, Mr. President. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I have seen this and you -- just a moment. Milos is telling me something. Momcilo MANDIC: Okay. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Have a good time. Momcilo MANDIC: Cheers. Milos: Momo. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Milos: Please, will you write down this house number. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. OK. And what is the last name? Okay give me just the house number. Milos: Babic Dusan, 81, Dolacka Street. Momcilo MANDIC: 81, Dolacka Street? Milos: Yes, he was captured yesterday on the 24th of June, 1992. Momcilo MANDIC: 21 Dolacka Street? Milos: 81. Momcilo MANDIC: 81. Milos: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: When was he captured? Milos: Yesterday, on the 24th of June, 1992. Momcilo MANDIC: 24 of June, 1992, captured? Milos: About 7.00 p.m. Momcilo MANDIC: Okay. Milos: Apparently the MUP men some three cars, my house, his house ... his house was searched and he was captured and so on. Momcilo MANDIC: Okay. Milos: I ask you kindly. Momcilo MANDIC: Okay. Milos: Please do something. He is my brother. Momcilo MANDIC: Okay, okay. Milos: And then is he for exchange. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Milos: I want to take everyone from there, my sisters-in-law, sister, brother-in-law and then let them set things on fire, loot there and do whatever they want. Momcilo MANDIC: Okay. Okay. I will put them on a list and we will finish that. Milos: Here are the names of the others. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, give me their names. Milos: Savic Zorka. Momcilo MANDIC: Savic Zorka. Milos: Savic Dunja. Momcilo MANDIC: Savic Zorka, Dunja. Milos: Yes. Cucilo Nedjeljko. Momcilo MANDIC: Cucilo Nedjeljko? Milos: No, yes, and Cucilo Slavojka, that is my sister. Momcilo MANDIC: Cucilo Slavojka. Milos: Yes. There are also Dolacka street, these two, Dolacka 83. Momcilo MANDIC: Okay. Milos: Oh, sorry, 63. Momcilo MANDIC: All 63, Dolacka Street? Milos: These two last on the list, they are all in Dolacka Street. Momcilo MANDIC: Okay. Milos: Please do something. Momcilo MANDIC: We'll be in touch. Milos: Long live!

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No inconsistencies identified by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're concerned just about one item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which is -- I appreciate Your Honour's question initially to the interpreters, but we're concerned about the item which in the English is at page 2 of 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: About three-quarters of the way down, does Your Honour see Mr. Mandic "yes, and the men they've already been transferred there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the B/C/S it's the penultimate item on the second page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But we're simply concerned to ensure -- perhaps we might test that and see what interpretation we receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You put a marker here. Are there any specific questions on that portion, Mr. Tieger? If not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There may be, Your Honour. I'm not entirely sure I understand the nature of Mr. Stewart's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you noted the translators are not able to follow the speaker, because of the speech. So the translation is done on the basis of the transcript. And then the other interpreter would listen to the voice and see whether there's any inconsistency, because it's an indirect translation of the text. So if you would have any questions about that specific part, then I'd like it to be replayed, that specific portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, our concern was just we're not happy with the English translation of the B/C/S that appears in the written exhibit. It's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the written exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the written exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like -- yes. Then I'd like to invite Ms. Cmeric -- that's not an inconsistency, but a translation issue. Ms. Cmeric would you please read the line just referred to by Mr. Stewart, and could I ask the interpreters then to translate that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The line is: [Interpretation] Yes, and the people are, already crossing over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that the major difference is that they are already crossing rather than being transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite a difference, in fact. Your Honour sees exactly the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you please keep in mind that the translation we now receive is a bit different from --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is a conversation between you and Mr. Krajisnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik brings your attention to Milos Savic's brother. First of all, who is Milos Savic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Savic is, I think, or rather, was President Krajisnik's secretary or member of his staff. I don't remember exactly which post he held. So he was an aide to Mr. Krajisnik in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Savic understood that his brother and members of his brother's family had been arrested and were being held on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And apparently Mr. Savic sought Mr. Krajisnik's assistance in getting them released and Mr. Krajisnik contacted you. Why did Mr. Krajisnik contact you to obtain Mr. Savic's release?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd better ask Mr. Krajisnik that. But I think that Mr. Krajisnik had known that the president of the commission, or rather, that the state commission was carrying out the exchange and that one of the members was from the Ministry of Justice. Since I was one of his close associates and he trusted me, I believe that was the reason why he addressed me, and I had channels at my disposal to arrange for the release of the family of Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik understand that at that time you were functioning as a member of the commission or functioning as president of that commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that as the president of the Assembly he was informed about that, but he knew that he should ask someone from the government or from the Ministry of Justice should do him his favour. Probably as someone close to him, he appealed to me. I don't believe that Mr. Krajisnik thought very much about who was the member of the commission or who was not the member of the commission. That was not on his mind at the time when he made this call to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to address that in just a moment, but first, Mr. Mandic, I'd like to ask you: What were the channels at your disposal to arrange for the release of persons held in detention by Muslims, by the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, through the state commission, through Vanovac or Jusuf Pusina, or my former colleagues who remained in Sarajevo and with whom I maintained contacts through the war. I could have arranged for many things, such as exchange or to help people who were imprisoned at that problem [as interpreted] or encountering any other kinds of problems. You know, Mr. Prosecutor, for many years I was a policeman in Sarajevo or rather an official with the police and that I maintained contacts with all the people who remained in Sarajevo, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in this case, you indicated that you would attempt to effect the release of Mr. Savic's family by placing them on a list.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, among other things, I said that, that I will take that with the people who were in charge, and I think that was Vanovac, from the Ilidza commission, that he was the one who compiled the lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would go through the exchange process we've discussed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the ways and possibilities to release those people from custody. However, I think that it was done in agreement with someone - I cannot remember exactly who - from the federal part of Sarajevo. Probably I called some of my former colleagues, acquaintances, or friends who were ready to do me a favour and to send those people over to the Serbian side. I think that's how the exchange was carried out, or rather, the release of the Savic family. But I cannot remember all the details. Similarly, on several occasions, and you have the documents and the transcripts of conversations, Mr. Krajisnik requested us to find a friendly -- a Muslim who was a friend of Mr. Krajisnik, and he asked for his release in Sarajevo. So these were a kind of shortcut use by former friends to help each other, and you have all these transcripts, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, in this case your first reaction was to indicate to Mr. Krajisnik that you would put Mr. Savic's brother on a list for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that it was not on Mr. Krajisnik's mind whether you were part of the Exchange Commission. Can you tell me, then, what he's referring to when he says during the conversation - and that's on page 3 of the English transcript, after a discussion about Boljakov potok?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I find on the top of page 3, the first line, I find language which is difficult for me to understand. I would first like to check whether that is a correct translation of -- it could well be, but we find that in the B/C/S original box, the sixth box on the third page, where it reads -- my pronunciation will be wrong [B/C/S spoken] That's the line. Have the interpreters found that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please translate that line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Since you are on this commission, Savic Dusan."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what my recollection is, that I heard, and that's not exactly the same as what's written in English on the first line of page 3. Mr. Tieger, it reads in my translation "since are in that commission," which makes it unclear who are on that commission, and now in English it says "since you are in that commission."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The word ti being you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Is it clear to you, Mr. Tieger, what --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And since the Court has just drawn our attention to that part of the conversation, Mr. Mandic:

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik making a reference to the Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. But Mr. Krajisnik is the person who will be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you understood -- or did you understand, Mr. Mandic, that Mr. Krajisnik was contacting you because he understood that you were a member of or part of that commission and could therefore effect that release?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not wishing to object to that question at all, but before the question is answered, we observe that a similar point is touched on in the English on page 3 of the transcript of the intercept, just below halfway down. And since this particular point is now specifically the focus of questioning, Ms. Cmeric suggests, because obviously we weren't focusing specifically on that, that if we could possibly hear that bit of the intercept, so we can see exactly what's said there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be possible to do that during the next break? We might not finish with the witness anyhow today, and if there would be anything else -- we have clarified the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We need it to be done before the question is answered, Your Honour. Otherwise I would accept Your Honour's suggestion completely, but that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is there any -- Your Honour, we've played it. I understand from the interpreters' booth there are no significant problems. Unless there's understood to be some problem with this portion, I suggest we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We don't know whether there is, is the answer and we'd like to clarify. We think there may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was about the first time -- I mean I perhaps disturbed a bit the course of the evidence because I was pointing at, well, some 15 lines higher up, a similar reference, which was not clear to me. Your question was about that first reference, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Either reference will do, Your Honour. But it is correct that my question was initially directed to the reference that counsel is pointing to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understood that. The question -- the I'm trying to say as little as possible since everybody including the witness is in court, Your Honour, that we wish to clarify what exactly the second reference says, so that the two references together in the document can be understood, before the question is, well, put, as it has been, and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be possible to play that part. Could you find it? Is that very difficult? So that there's no question about any ... From what I -- I don't know who is playing. Are the technicians involved or ...? Let me do it in a different way. You can do it during the break. I'm not asking it to be played at this moment. Mr. Mandic, part of the transcript says that the first time that Mr. Krajisnik raises the issue of the arrest of Milos Savic and then I take it that he wants to refer to family members of him, your answer was yes. And then the next part was: "Since you are in that commission ..." How did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik wasn't interested personally in who the people were in the Exchange Commission. He knew that I was minister of justice and that it was up to me to propose the members of the commission and that I was doing that job. So he -- what he instructed me to do was along those lines, that I should do what needed to be done, and that is, to save the Savic family and pull them out the of imprisonment. So Mr. Krajisnik wasn't saying this to me as a member of the commission, but as minister of justice. And he saw me as being the embodiment of the whole commission. Because as president of the Assembly, he wasn't interested in what the individuals did. I was the first man in the ministry, Ministry of Justice, so it was up to me to do what he told me. Whether I was going to do it by looking at some lists or effecting the change in some other way, he wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stoup, Mr. Mandic. So you say that where he makes reference to the commission, he, in your understanding, had on his mind the commission of exchange, and you understood it not to be a reference to you being a member of the commission? Yes? You were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not a member of the commission, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But to your involvement with the work of that commission as minister.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic, for these answers. If there's any -- we have now clarified the first entry where the commission appears. If there's any need, the parties can check through the videotape and assist each other to see whether the second reference to the commission brings any new light or brings any further -- whether it would raise any need for further questions in that respect. Yes, Mr. Stewart. It's a quarter to 2.00, so I'm about to adjourn. Nothing special?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was standing up acknowledging and hearing what Your Honour was saying on that point. So I'll quietly sit down again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, we'll adjourn for the day. Tomorrow we'll not sit in the morning. We'll sit in the afternoon. We'll start at a quarter past 2.00 and we'll be in Courtroom III. We adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 26th day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
